name: Chile
summary: A long, narrow republic on the Pacific coast of South America, independent since 1818, with a military dictatorship from 1973 to 1990.

knownFor.label: Copper mining
knownFor.note: Chile is the world’s largest copper producer.

knownFor.label: Atacama observatories
knownFor.note: Some of the world’s largest telescopes.

location.value: Long, narrow country on South America's Pacific coast.

terrain.value: The Atacama Desert in the north, the Andes along the east, and fjords along the southern coast.

climate.value: From the world’s driest desert in the north, through a Mediterranean centre, to an oceanic climate with glaciers in the south.

resources.value: Copper (the world’s largest producer in 2019), lithium (second largest) and nitrates (historically).

disasters.value: Earthquakes, such as the magnitude 8.8 earthquake of February 2010.

urbanisation.value: About 85% urban; 40% live in Greater Santiago.

disease.value: Good public health compared with the region.

migration.value: About 1.5 million Latin American immigrants (8% of the population in 2019), mainly from Venezuela, Peru and Haiti.

economicBase.value: Relies heavily on copper mining exports.

tradeRoutes.value: Free trade agreements with many countries, including the United States (2004).

wealth.value: A high-income economy and one of South America’s most stable nations.

inequality.value: Nationwide protests (2019–22) over fares, living costs, privatisation and inequality.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic under the 1981 constitution (in force 11 March 1981). The republic was declared in 1818.

keyRulers.value: Bernardo O’Higgins. Salvador Allende. Augusto Pinochet. Michelle Bachelet.

succession.value: Elected governments, interrupted by the 1973 coup; democracy returned in 1990.

institutions.value: A bicameral National Congress (Senate and Chamber of Deputies), a Constitutional Court and a Supreme Court.

stability.value: Military dictatorship under Pinochet (1973–90), with more than 3,000 deaths and disappearances.

eliteConflict.value: Severe left–right polarisation in the 1960s and 1970s.

armyAndTech.value: Described as among the most professional armies in Latin America.

majorWars.value: War of the Pacific (1879–83) against Peru and Bolivia.

territoryChange.value: Gained its northern territory and nitrate deposits in the War of the Pacific (1879–83), ending Bolivia’s access to the sea.

alliancesRivals.value: A naval arms race and border disputes with Argentina, settled by British arbitration in 1902.

openness.value: Free-trade agreement with the United States signed in 2003.

communicationTransport.value: A railway system; the Santiago Metro (1975).

religion.value: About 54% Catholic and 26% with no religion (2024 census).

languageWriting.value: Spanish is the official and national language.

artsArchitecture.value: Nobel Prize-winning poets Gabriela Mistral (1945) and Pablo Neruda (1971).

socialStructure.value: The Mapuche, nearly two million people, are the largest Indigenous group.

dailyLife.value: Cuisine featuring seafood, beef, fruit and vegetables.

colonisation.value: Conquered by Spain from 1540 and part of the Spanish Empire until independence.

declineSignals.value: Protests in 2019–22 led to a constitutional process.
